science.text:
(i) State Ohm's law. Draw the V–I graph of a conductor that obeys Ohm's law, and show that the slope of this graph gives the resistance of the conductor. (3)
(ii) Three resistors R1, R2 and R3 are joined in series. Derive the expression for their equivalent resistance. (2)
science.answer:
(i) Ohm's law: the potential difference V across the ends of a metallic wire in a circuit is directly proportional to the current I flowing through it, provided its temperature stays the same (V ∝ I, so V = IR) (1).
Graph (1): V (volts) on the y-axis and current I (ampere) on the x-axis; a straight line through the origin. Mark two points A and B on the line and complete the right-angled triangle ABC (AC horizontal, BC vertical).
Slope = BC/AC = V/I = R. So the slope of the V–I graph gives the resistance (1).
(ii) Circuit diagram (½): R1, R2, R3 joined end to end between X and Y, with a battery, key K and ammeter A in series, and a voltmeter V across XY. Let I be the current and V the total potential difference.
Potential differences: V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2, V3 = IR3 (½).
If Rs is the equivalent resistance, V = IRs. The total potential difference is the sum: V = V1 + V2 + V3 (½)
IRs = IR1 + IR2 + IR3, so Rs = R1 + R2 + R3 (½).

science.text:
A diagram shows a thick leaf with notches along its margin. Small buds (labelled adventitious buds) sit in the marginal notches, and at one notch a young plant with tiny leaves is growing from the leaf. (5)
(i) Name the structure and the type of reproduction shown. (1)
(ii) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this method of reproduction. (2)
(iii) Give the reason: asexual reproduction does not produce genetic variation. (1)
(iv) Why have higher organisms taken up sexual reproduction even though it is complicated? (1)
science.answer:
(i) Structure: Bryophyllum leaf (½); type: vegetative propagation / asexual reproduction. (½)
(ii) Advantage: the new plants are genetically identical to the parent and keep its desirable characters. (1)
Disadvantage: there is no genetic variation. (1)
(iii) Only the DNA of a single parent is involved and there is no fusion of gametes (the offspring are formed by mitosis), so they have the same genetic make-up as the parent. (1)
(iv) Sexual reproduction creates genetic variation, which improves the chances of survival in a changing environment and drives evolution. (1)

science.text:
(i) Name the compound formed when ethanol is heated at 443 K with concentrated H₂SO₄, and draw its electron dot structure. What is the role of concentrated H₂SO₄ in this reaction?

(i) Ethene, C₂H₄ (½)
Electron dot structure (draw): the two carbon atoms share two pairs of electrons (a double bond, four dots between the C atoms), and each carbon shares one pair with each of its two hydrogen atoms. (1)
Concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as a dehydrating agent. (½)
(ii) Hydrogenation is the reaction in which unsaturated hydrocarbons (compounds) add hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst such as nickel or palladium to give saturated hydrocarbons. (1)
R₂C=CR₂ + H₂ →(Ni catalyst) R₂CH–CHR₂ (1)
Use in industry: hydrogenation of vegetable oils, which turns them into fats with saturated carbon chains. (1)

sst.text: Describe any three features of the rabi crop season. (3)
sst.answer:
(i) Rabi crops are sown in winter, from October to December, and harvested in summer, from April to June. (1)
(ii) Important rabi crops are wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. (1)
(iii) These crops are grown in large parts of India; the north and north-western states such as Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh are important for wheat and other rabi crops. (1)
(iv) Winter rain from western temperate cyclones helps these crops succeed. (1)
(v) The success of the Green Revolution in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan has also helped. (1)
(Any three, 1 mark each.)

sst.text: Explain why the Sri Lankan Tamils began to feel more and more alienated from 1956 onwards. (2)
sst.answer:
1. In 1956 a law was passed that made Sinhala the only official language of Sri Lanka, ignoring Tamil. (1)
2. The governments followed preferential policies that favoured Sinhala-speaking applicants for university places and government jobs. (1)
3. The new constitution laid down that the state would protect and foster Buddhism, the religion of most Sinhalas. (1)
4. Through these majoritarian policies the Sinhala-led government ignored the interests of the Tamils. (1)
(Write any two.)

sst.text: Explain 'secularism' as laid down in the Indian Constitution. (2)
sst.answer:
1. There is no official religion for the Indian state. (1)
2. The Constitution gives all individuals and communities the freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion. (1)
3. The Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion. (1)
4. The Constitution allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities. (1)
(Write any two.)

sst.text: Distinguish between formal and informal sources of credit. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Formal credit includes loans from banks and cooperatives. Informal credit includes loans from traders, moneylenders and relatives. (1)
2. Formal sources charge a lower rate of interest. Informal sources charge a high rate of interest. (1)
3. The Reserve Bank of India supervises the working of formal sources. No organisation supervises the lending of informal sources. (1)
(Write any three points of difference.)

sst.text: Suggest any two reforms to strengthen the party system in India. (2)
sst.answer:
1. Internal democracy within parties should be strengthened. (1)
2. The growing role of money and muscle power should be checked. (1)
3. Parties should offer meaningful choices to the voters. (1)
4. Ordinary party workers should get a chance to rise to power. (1)
5. It should be made compulsory for parties to give a minimum number of tickets, about one-third, to women candidates. (1)
6. Citizens, pressure groups, movements and the media can put pressure on parties to overcome their challenges. (1)
7. The party system should be able to accommodate social and regional divisions. (1)
8. India should strengthen its multi-party system, keeping in mind its social and geographical diversity. (1)
(Write any two.)

science.text:
(a) Why are the organisms of the first trophic level important in any food chain? (1)
(b) Justify: 'The flow of energy in an ecosystem is in one direction only (unidirectional).' (1)
science.answer:
(a) Organisms of the first trophic level (producers) fix the sun's energy and make it available to the heterotrophs (consumers). (1)
(b) As energy moves on through the trophic levels, it is no longer available to the level before. The energy captured by the autotrophs does not go back to the solar input, and the energy passed to the herbivores does not come back to the autotrophs. (1)

The precipitate is barium sulphate, BaSO₄. Its ions are Ba²⁺ (½) and SO₄²⁻ (½)

science.text: In the ray diagram, a horizontal line is the boundary between medium 1 (above) and medium 2 (below), and NN′ is the normal at the point O. A ray AO in medium 1 falls on O, making an angle of 30° with the boundary surface. The refracted ray OB goes into medium 2 and makes an angle of 30° with the normal. Using this diagram, calculate the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1. (Take √3 = 1.732) (2)
science.answer:
Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r (½)
The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: ∠i = 90° − 30° = 60°; ∠r = 30°.
n = sin 60° / sin 30° (1)
n = (√3/2) / (1/2) = √3 = 1.732 (½).

science.answer:
(i) Sodium (½) and potassium (½) (lithium is also correct).
Observations: the reaction is violent; a large amount of heat is given out; the gas given off may catch fire. (½ each = 1½)
(ii) The gas is hydrogen. Bring a burning matchstick (or splinter) near the gas (the bubbles): it burns with a pop sound. (½)

science.text:
Keeping the right and left sides of the heart apart stops oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing, and different animals have different kinds of heart. A table gives four columns: organisms, number of chambers in the heart, type of blood circulated, type of circulation. Row 1: Fish, (i) ____, mixed, single circulation. Row 2: (ii) ____, 3-chambered, mixed, incomplete double circulation. Row 3: Birds and mammals, 4-chambered, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood kept on separate paths, (iii) ____.
(I) Fill in the blanks (i), (ii) and (iii). (1½)
(II) Which type of circulation is the most efficient? (½)
science.answer:
(I) (i) 2-chambered (½)
(ii) Amphibians / reptiles (½)
(iii) Double circulation (½)
(II) Double circulation. (½)
Note: the paper's table writes 'mixed' blood for fish. By NCERT the two-chambered fish heart carries only deoxygenated blood: it pumps blood to the gills, and the oxygenated blood goes straight from the gills to the body (blood passes through the heart only once).

sst.text: Explain how democracies lead to a peaceful and harmonious life among citizens. (5)
sst.answer:
1. Democracies try to produce a harmonious social life. (1)
2. Democracies can accommodate various social divisions better. (1)
3. Democracies usually develop a procedure for their competition, which reduces the chance of tensions becoming explosive or violent. (1)
4. Democracies are better able to develop mechanisms to handle and negotiate social differences, divisions and conflicts. (1)
5. Democracy is not simply rule by majority opinion. (1)
6. The majority works with the minority so that governments represent the general view. (1)
7. Democracy promotes the dignity and freedom of individuals. (1)
8. It promotes equality among citizens. (1)
9. It improves the quality of decision making. (1)
10. It provides a method to resolve conflicts. (1)
(Write any five.)

sst.text: Explain the role of Self-Help Groups in rural society. (5 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Self-Help Groups (SHGs) are a way of giving loans to the rural poor. (1)
2. The rural poor, especially women, are organised into small groups that pool their savings. (1)
3. Each member saves from Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more, depending on what she can save. (1)
4. Members can take small loans from the group itself to meet their needs. (1)
5. The bank gives a loan in the name of the group, meant to create self-employment for the members. (1)
6. The group members take most of the important decisions on savings and loans. (1)
7. The group decides the purpose and amount of each loan, the interest to be charged and the repayment schedule. (1)
8. If any member does not repay, the other members follow it up seriously. (1)
9. Because of this, banks are willing to lend to poor women organised in SHGs even though they have no collateral. (1)
(Write any five points.)

sst.text: Explain why sharing of power is desirable in a democracy. (3)
sst.answer:
1. It reduces the chances of conflict between social groups. (1)
2. It is the very spirit of democracy. (1)
3. It ensures the stability of the political order. (1)
4. In a democracy, power is shared with those who are affected by its use. (1)
5. People have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. (1)
6. Power sharing brings better outcomes. (1)
7. It gives the system legitimacy, because citizens who take part acquire a stake in it. (1)
8. Power sharing is valuable in itself. (1)
(Write any three.)

sst.chapter: E2 Sectors of the Indian Economy
sst.text: Describe the growing importance of the tertiary sector in the Indian economy. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. The tertiary sector has become the largest producing sector in India. (1)
2. It provides basic services such as hospitals, educational institutions and postal services. (1)
3. The growth of the primary and secondary sectors has increased the demand for tertiary sector services such as transport, trade and storage. (1)
4. Rising incomes have pushed the demand for services up even further. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.chapter: H5 Print Culture and the Modern World
sst.text:
Source on 'Print and Censorship' (in short: before 1798 the East India Company was not much concerned with censorship; its first controls were aimed at Englishmen in India who criticised Company misrule. By the 1820s the Calcutta Supreme Court made regulations to control press freedom and the Company encouraged newspapers praising British rule; in 1835 Governor-General Bentinck agreed to revise the press laws and Thomas Macaulay framed rules that restored the earlier freedoms).
(8.1) Why were the Company's officials worried about what was being printed? (1)
(8.2) Explain the main step the East India Company took to control the freedom of the press. (1)
(8.3) Explain the role of printing in the spread of nationalism during India's freedom movement. (2)
sst.answer:
(8.1) They worried that the criticism might be used by the Company's critics in England to attack its trade monopoly in India. (1)
(8.2) By the 1820s, the Calcutta Supreme Court passed regulations to control press freedom, and the Company began encouraging newspapers that would celebrate British rule. (1) [The scheme also accepts: the Vernacular Press Act. That Act was passed by the British government in 1878, not by the Company.]
(8.3) Any two:
1. Nationalist newspapers grew in number in all parts of India; they reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities. (1)
2. Newspapers carried news from one place to another and connected people, creating a pan-Indian identity. (1)
3. Nationalist feeling was spread through images, songs, newspapers, articles, pamphlets and so on. (1)
4. When Punjab revolutionaries were deported in 1907, Balgangadhar Tilak wrote about them with great sympathy in his Kesari; this led to his imprisonment in 1908, which provoked widespread protests across India. (1)

science.answer:
(i) Placenta. (1)
Structure: it is a disc embedded in the wall of the uterus. It has villi on the embryo's side, and on the mother's side there are blood spaces surrounding the villi. (1)
Functions besides nutrition:
• It removes the wastes made by the embryo. (½)
• It provides a large surface area for oxygen to pass from the mother to the embryo. (½)

sst.text: "The Civil Disobedience Movement became a mass movement." Explain this statement with examples. (5)
sst.answer:
1. The Civil Disobedience Movement began in 1930 with Gandhiji's Salt March to Dandi, where he broke the salt law, after Lord Irwin rejected his eleven demands. (1)
2. Gandhiji found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation; the demands were kept wide-ranging so that all classes of Indian society could identify with them. (1)
3. The Salt March united diverse groups; thousands of people in different parts of the country broke the salt law and demonstrated in front of government salt factories. (1)
4. As the movement spread, foreign cloth was boycotted and liquor shops were picketed. (1)
5. Peasants refused to pay the chaukidari tax and village officials resigned. (1)
6. In many places forest people violated forest laws. (1)
7. In the countryside, rich peasant communities such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh were active in the movement. (1)
8. As producers of commercial crops they were hard hit by the trade depression and falling prices. (1)
9. The government's refusal to reduce the revenue demand caused widespread resentment, and these rich peasants became enthusiastic supporters of the movement. (1)

sst.text: Explain any five ways of reducing industrial pollution. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) Use less water for processing by reusing and recycling it in two or more stages. (1)
(ii) Harvest rainwater to meet water needs. (1)
(iii) Treat hot water and effluents before releasing them into rivers and ponds, in three stages: primary treatment by mechanical means (screening, grinding, flocculation, sedimentation), secondary treatment by biological processes, and tertiary treatment by biological, chemical and physical processes, which recycles the waste water. (1)
(iv) Regulate by law the overdrawing of groundwater by industries where groundwater is under threat. (1)
(v) Reduce particulate matter in the air by fitting smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators; reduce smoke by using oil or gas instead of coal. (1)
(vi) Fit generators with silencers. (1)
(vii) Redesign machinery to raise energy efficiency and reduce noise. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)

sst.text: Explain how democracy is a better form of government than dictatorship. (5)
sst.answer:
1. Non-democratic rulers need not bother about deliberation, majorities or public opinion; they may take decisions the people do not accept and so may face problems. (1)
2. A democratic government takes more time because it follows procedures, but this makes sure decisions are based on norms and procedures. (1)
3. Transparency is often missing in a non-democratic government, while democracy is transparent. (1)
4. Democracy can be expected to produce a government that follows procedures and is accountable to the people, unlike a dictatorship. (1)
5. Democracy develops mechanisms for citizens to hold the government accountable and to take part in decision making whenever they think fit. (1)
6. Respect for women and equal treatment of women are necessary parts of a democratic society. (1)
7. Non-democratic regimes often ignore or suppress internal social differences, while democracies can handle social differences, divisions and conflicts. (1)
(Write any five.)

sst.chapter: E4 Globalisation and the Indian Economy
sst.text: 'Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries.' Explain this statement with examples. (5 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Globalisation has encouraged foreign investment. (1)
2. MNCs set up production close to markets, where skilled and unskilled labour is available at low cost. (1)
3. MNCs choose countries whose policies make operations easy. (1)
4. MNCs set up production jointly with local companies. (1)
5. Technology is exchanged better between countries, which benefits people. (1)
6. Interdependence between countries has increased. (1)
7. Consumers have more access to products from across the world. (1)
8. Markets of different countries become integrated. (1)
9. Countries become culturally richer. (1)
10. Examples: Cargill Foods, a large American MNC, bought the Indian company Parakh Foods and became the largest producer of edible oil in India; Ford Motors set up a large plant near Chennai with Mahindra and Mahindra, exports cars to South Africa, Mexico and Brazil and supplies car parts to its plants abroad; Indian companies such as Tata Motors, Infosys and Ranbaxy have themselves become MNCs working across the world. (1)
(Write any five points.)

sst.text:
Source subject: Sacred groves, a wealth of rare species. In short: tribal people believe all creations of nature must be protected, so some forest patches (sacred groves, the forests of gods and goddesses) are left untouched; some communities revere particular trees, such as the mahua and kadamba of the Mundas and Santhals, and the tamarind and mango of tribals of Odisha and Bihar.
(35.1) How do sacred groves show the link between spirituality and ecology? (1)
(35.2) How do tribal practices help in conserving forests? (1)
(35.3) Why is the conservation of wildlife important for us? (2)
sst.answer:
(35.1) Sacred qualities are given to springs, mountain peaks, plants and animals, and so they are closely protected; in many communities mountains, plants and animals are worshipped. (Any one) (1)
(35.2) The Mundas and Santhals of the Chota Nagpur region worship the mahua and kadamba trees; tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship the tamarind and mango trees during weddings, so these trees are protected. (Any one) (1)
(35.3) (i) It maintains the ecological balance. (1)
(ii) It preserves ecological diversity. (1)
(iii) It preserves our life support system. (1)
(Any two, 1 mark each.)

science.text: We do not clean ponds and lakes, but an aquarium has to be cleaned regularly. Why? (2)
science.answer:
An aquarium is a man-made ecosystem. It has no natural cleaning agents such as decomposers, so it has to be cleaned from time to time. (1)
Ponds and lakes are natural ecosystems; they have natural cleaning agents (decomposers) that break down the wastes. (1)

science.chapter: Ch 10 The Human Eye and the Colourful World
science.text: A person has an eye defect in which the far point of the eye has come nearer than infinity. Name the defect. Give its two main causes. Draw a ray diagram to show how this defect is corrected with a suitable lens. (3)
science.answer:
Defect: myopia (short-sightedness) (1).
Two causes:
• the eye lens has too much curvature (½);
• the eyeball has become longer than normal (½).
Ray diagram (1): show a concave (diverging) lens placed in front of the eye. Rays coming from a distant object (from infinity) pass through the concave lens, spread out as if they came from the far point of the eye, and then the eye lens brings them to focus on the retina.

science.chapter: Ch 12 Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
science.text: What is a fuse used for in household electric circuits? How is its job different from the job of the green wire in household circuits? What will happen if an electrician fits a fuse of a higher rating than the one prescribed for a circuit? (3)
science.answer:
Fuse: it protects the appliances from overloading (and short-circuiting) (1).
Green wire: it is the earth wire. It gives a low-resistance path for current to flow to the earth if current leaks to the metal body of an appliance, and so it prevents electric shock (1).
A fuse of higher rating will not melt when the current rises above the safe limit, so it will not be able to protect the circuit during overloading; the appliances and wiring may get damaged (1).

sst.text: Why did the Non-Cooperation Movement spread from the cities to the countryside? Explain. (5)
sst.answer:
1. The movement drew the struggles of peasants and tribals into its fold. (1)
2. In Awadh, the peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra, a sanyasi. (1)
3. Here the peasants' movement was against the talukdars and landlords, who demanded very high rents and a variety of other cesses from them. (1)
4. Peasants had to do begar, that is, work on the landlords' farms without any payment. (1)
5. The peasant movement demanded a reduction of revenue and the abolition of begar. (1)
6. Kisan Sabhas were formed. (1)
7. In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, tribal peasants led by Alluri Sitaram Raju started a militant guerrilla movement because the colonial government had closed large forest areas to them. (1)
8. In Assam, plantation workers were not allowed to leave the tea gardens without permission (Inland Emigration Act of 1859); on hearing of the movement, thousands of them defied the authorities and left for home. (1)

sst.text: Analyse the importance of democracy in reducing poverty and inequality. (5)
sst.answer:
1. Democracy promotes political equality through universal adult franchise (one person, one vote). (1)
2. It raises the dignity of individuals by treating them as citizens, not subjects. (1)
3. It improves the quality of decisions through debate and discussion. (1)
4. It leaves room to correct mistakes. (1)
5. Many Central and State government schemes have been started to reduce disparity. (1)
6. Reservation has helped to uplift the marginalised sections. (1)
(Write any five.)

sst.text: Analyse why political parties are needed in a democracy. (3)
sst.answer:
1. Political parties are the most visible institutions in a democracy; for most ordinary citizens, democracy means political parties. (1)
2. A political party is a group of people who contest elections and hold power in the government. (1)
3. The rise of parties is directly linked to the rise of representative democracy, which large societies need. (1)
4. As societies became large and complex, they needed some agency to gather different views on various issues and present them to the government. (1)
5. They needed a way to bring various representatives together so that a responsible government could be formed. (1)
6. They needed a mechanism to support or restrain the government, make policies, and justify or oppose them. (1)
7. So parties are a necessary condition for a democracy. (1)
8. Without parties every candidate would be independent; no one could promise major policy changes, and no one would be responsible for how the country is run. (1)
(Write any three.)

sst.chapter: H5 Print Culture and the Modern World
sst.text:
Source on 'Print and Censorship' (in short: the colonial government kept a continuous watch on all books and newspapers published in India and passed many laws to control the press. In the First World War, under the Defence of India Rules, 22 newspapers had to furnish securities and 18 of them shut down; the Sedition Committee under Rowlatt (1919) tightened control further, and in the Second World War the Defence of India Act allowed war reports, including those on the Quit India Movement, to be censored, so about 90 newspapers were suppressed in August 1942).
(34.1) What method did the colonial government use to keep track of Indian newspapers? (1)
(34.2) How did the colonial government's laws affect the press? (1)
(34.3) Analyse the effect of the Sedition Committee on newspapers. (2)
sst.answer:
(34.1) Any one: the government passed the Vernacular Press Act and other laws to control the press; it imposed penalties; it kept a regular track of vernacular newspapers; it censored reports on war-related topics. (1)
(34.2) Any one: under the Defence of India Rules in the First World War, 22 newspapers had to furnish securities and 18 of them shut down; Indians protested strongly; the liberty of the press was lost; many people were imprisoned for breaking these laws. (1)
(34.3)
1. The Sedition Committee under Rowlatt (1919) further strengthened the government's control over the press. (1)
2. This led to penalties being imposed on various newspapers. (1)
3. When a report was judged to be seditious, the newspaper was warned; if the warning was ignored, the press could be seized and its printing machinery confiscated. (1)

sst.text: Analyse the role of credit in the development of a nation. (5 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Credit makes investment in business possible and helps people start new business ventures. (1)
2. Credit helps build infrastructure, which strengthens the whole economy. (1)
3. It raises the production capacity of entrepreneurs and companies, which raises their profits and the overall standard of living. (1)
4. It helps producers meet the running expenses of production and finish production on time. (1)
5. It helps consumers make big purchases such as homes, vehicles and gadgets. (1)
6. It lets farmers buy better seeds, fertilisers and equipment, which raises crop yields and improves farming. (1)
7. It funds research and development, leading to new inventions. (1)
(Write any five points.)

science.chapter: Ch 10 The Human Eye and the Colourful World
science.text: What is a rainbow? Draw a diagram, with labels, to show how a rainbow is formed. (3)
science.answer:
A rainbow is a natural spectrum of sunlight that appears in the sky after rain (1).
Labelled diagram (2): draw a raindrop (circle) with sunlight falling on it. At entry the light is refracted and split into colours (dispersion); the colours are reflected from the inside back surface of the drop (internal reflection); they are refracted again as they come out of the drop. Label: sunlight, raindrop, and the two outgoing colours red and violet.

science.text: Why is the change of ethanol into ethanoic acid called an oxidation reaction? Name the oxidising agent used for this change, and write the chemical equation for it. How is this reaction different from the burning of ethanol in oxygen? (3)
science.answer:
Oxygen is added to ethanol to give ethanoic acid, so it is oxidation. (½)
Oxidising agent: alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate. (½)
CH₃–CH₂OH →(alkaline KMnO₄ + heat, or acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ + heat) CH₃COOH (1)
Here ethanol is only partly oxidised, by an oxidising agent, to ethanoic acid. When ethanol burns in oxygen it undergoes combustion: it is completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, and heat and light are given out. (1)

science.text: "Every organism has two sets of all genes, one from each parent, so both parents contribute equally to the DNA of the offspring in sexual reproduction." If so, how does the DNA of the species stay stable (the same amount from generation to generation)? Discuss. (3)
science.answer:
• Each cell has two copies of each chromosome, one from the male parent and one from the female parent. (1)
• Each germ cell (gamete) takes only one chromosome from each pair (either the maternal or the paternal one). (1)
• When two germ cells fuse, the normal number of chromosomes is restored in the offspring, so the DNA of the species stays stable. (1)

science.text:
(i) State Ohm's law. (1)
(ii) Three resistors R1, R2 and R3 are joined in parallel. Derive the expression for their equivalent resistance. (2)
(iii) Two wires A and B have exactly the same shape and size but are made of different materials. Their V–I graphs (potential difference V on the y-axis, current I on the x-axis) are two straight lines starting from the origin; the line for B is steeper than the line for A. Which of A and B is the better choice for making a heating element? Give a reason. (2)
science.answer:
(i) Ohm's law: the potential difference V across the ends of a metallic wire in a circuit is directly proportional to the current flowing through it, provided its temperature stays the same (1).
(ii) Circuit diagram (½): R1, R2 and R3 joined in parallel between two points, connected to a battery and a key; the main current I divides into I1, I2, I3 in the three resistors. The potential difference V is the same across each.
Currents: I1 = V/R1, I2 = V/R2, I3 = V/R3 (½)
If Rp is the equivalent resistance, I = V/Rp. The main current is the sum: I = I1 + I2 + I3 (½)
V/Rp = V/R1 + V/R2 + V/R3, so 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (½).
(iii) Wire B (1).
Reason: the slope of the V–I graph is V/I = R; B has the larger slope, so its resistance is more. Both wires have the same length and area, and R = ρ l / A, so the resistivity of B is more. High resistivity is what a heating element needs (1).

science.text: "Variation helps a species to survive over time." Explain this with an example. (2)
science.answer: Variation gives a species a chance to survive when the environment becomes unfavourable or changes. For example, suppose a population of bacteria lives in temperate waters and the water temperature rises because of global warming. Most of the bacteria would die, but the few variants that can resist heat would survive and grow further. (2)

sst.text: Suggest any two ways to increase the representation of women in leadership roles. (2)
sst.answer:
1. Increase training programmes for women. (1)
2. Increase mentorship programmes. (1)
3. Improve career and educational opportunities for women. (1)
4. Develop different skills among women. (1)
5. Implement laws like the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (Women's Reservation Act, 2023) effectively. (1)
(Write any two.)

sst.chapter: H3 The Making of a Global World
sst.text: In what way were the silk routes an example of lively pre-modern trade? Explain. (3)
sst.answer:
1. There were several silk routes over land and by sea, linking vast regions of Asia with Europe and northern Africa. (1)
2. Chinese silk cargoes travelling west passed along these routes. (1)
3. Chinese pottery, and textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia, also travelled along the silk routes. (1)
4. In return, precious metals, gold and silver, flowed from Europe to Asia. (1)

sst.text: Describe the main features of commercial farming in India. (3)
sst.answer:
(i) Large amounts of modern inputs are used, such as high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides. (1)
(ii) It gives higher productivity. (1)
(iii) How commercial the farming is differs from one region to another. (1)
(iv) Example: rice is a commercial crop in Haryana, but in Odisha it is a subsistence crop. (1)
(Any three, 1 mark each.)

sst.chapter: E4 Globalisation and the Indian Economy
sst.text: 'Improvement in technology has stimulated the globalisation process.' Explain this statement with examples. (5 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor that has stimulated globalisation. (1)
2. For example, the past fifty years have seen many improvements in transport technology. (1)
3. This has made delivery of goods over long distances much faster and cheaper. (1)
4. Even more remarkable are the developments in information and communication technology; telecommunications, computers and the Internet have been changing rapidly. (1)
5. Telecommunication facilities such as the telegraph, telephone (including mobile phones) and fax are used to contact one another around the world. (1)
6. The use of containers for transporting goods has led to huge reductions in port handling costs and increased the speed with which exports reach markets. (1)
7. The cost of air transport has fallen, so airlines now carry much larger volumes of goods. (1)
8. Through the Internet we can send instant e-mail and talk (voice-mail) across the world at negligible cost. (1)
(Write any five points.)

sst.text: "Minerals are an indispensable part of our lives." Justify this statement. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) Almost everything we use, from a tiny pin to a tall building or a big ship, is made from minerals. (1)
(ii) Railway lines and the tarmac of roads are made from minerals, which shows their role in infrastructure. (1)
(iii) Cars, buses, trains and aeroplanes are made from minerals and run on power resources taken from the earth. (1)
(iv) Even the food we eat contains minerals. (1)
(v) At every stage of development, people have used minerals for their livelihood, decoration, festivals and religious and ceremonial rites. (1)
(vi) Minerals give raw materials to many manufacturing industries and so help industrial development. (1)
(vii) Minerals support economic growth by creating jobs and adding to exports. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)

science.text:
A diagram shows three stages: first, a single cell with its nucleus and cytoplasm, enclosed in a cyst (protective wall); second, stage P, the same cyst now holding many small cells, each with its own nucleus; third, the cyst wall broken and the many small cells released. (5)
(i) Name the kind of reproduction shown and say what type of reproduction it is. (1)
(ii) Comment on what happens in stage P. (1)
(iii) Name one organism that reproduces in this way. (½)
(iv) Name the method used to raise plants that have lost the capacity to produce seeds, and give any two advantages of growing plants this way. (2½)
science.answer:
(i) Multiple fission (½); asexual reproduction. (½)
(ii) In stage P, the nucleus divides repeatedly and then the cytoplasm divides, so many daughter cells are formed at the same time. (1)
(iii) Plasmodium. (½)
(iv) Vegetative propagation. (½)
Advantages:
• All the plants produced are genetically similar to the parent plant. (1)
• Such plants flower and bear fruits earlier than plants grown from seeds. (1)

science.text: A student gets a sharp image of an object 3 cm tall on a white screen with a concave mirror of focal length 12 cm. The object is 18 cm from the mirror. Find: (i) how far the image is from the mirror; (ii) the height of the image. (3)
science.answer:
Data, with the New Cartesian sign convention: h = +3 cm, f = −12 cm, u = −18 cm (½).
(i) Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (½)
1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/(−12) − 1/(−18) = −1/12 + 1/18 (½)
= (−3 + 2)/36 = −1/36, so v = −36 cm. The image is 36 cm in front of the mirror (½).
(ii) h′ = −(v/u) × h (½)
h′ = −(−36/−18) × 3 cm = −6 cm. The image is 6 cm tall and inverted (½).

science.text:
(a) A figure shows one human nephron with its blood vessels: a capillary cluster (glomerulus) sitting inside a cup-shaped structure at the start of the tubule, then the coiled tubule and long loop wrapped in a network of capillaries, ending in the collecting duct. The label 'X' points to the cup-shaped structure that encloses the capillary cluster. Name 'X' and state its role in urine formation. (1)
(b) Why are some substances selectively taken back (reabsorbed) from the initial filtrate as it flows along the tubular part of the nephron? (1)
science.answer:
(a) X is Bowman's capsule. (½) It collects the filtrate (filtered from the blood in the glomerulus). (½)
(b) Reabsorption is selective because the body (nephron) adjusts it to how much excess water there is in the body, how much dissolved waste has to be removed, and how much useful substance has to be kept. (1)

sst.chapter: H3 The Making of a Global World
sst.text: How did the European empire spread into America in the sixteenth century? Explain. (2)
sst.answer:
1. The Europeans had superior fire power, but the conquest was not just a result of this. (1)
2. Their most powerful weapon was germs such as smallpox. The local people of America had no immunity against these diseases, which spread deep into the continent and wiped out whole communities, paving the way for conquest. (1)

sst.text: Explain the steps taken by the government to improve agriculture in India. (2)
sst.answer:
(i) Land reform was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan: collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari. (1)
(ii) Multipurpose projects were started, with dams and canals for irrigation, electricity and flood control. (1)
(iii) The Green Revolution (package technology) and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were started. (1)
(iv) In the 1980s and 1990s a comprehensive land development programme with both institutional and technical reforms was begun. (1)
(v) Crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease was provided. (1)
(vi) Grameen banks, cooperative societies and banks were set up to give farmers loans at lower interest. (1)
(vii) Schemes such as the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) and the Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS) were introduced. (1)
(viii) Special weather bulletins and farm programmes were started on radio and television. (1)
(ix) The government announces minimum support prices (MSP), remunerative and procurement prices for important crops, to protect farmers from speculators and middlemen. (1)
(Any two, 1 mark each.)

sst.chapter: H5 Print Culture and the Modern World
sst.text: Explain how print helped the spread of the Protestant Reformation. (3)
sst.answer:
1. The religious reformer Martin Luther wrote the Ninety-Five Theses criticising many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church. (1)
2. A printed copy was posted on a church door in Wittenberg, challenging the Church to debate his ideas. (1)
3. Luther's writings were immediately reproduced in large numbers and read widely. (1)
4. This led to a division within the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. (1)
5. Luther's translation of the New Testament sold many copies within a few weeks, and a second edition appeared within three months. (1)
6. Print created a new intellectual atmosphere and helped spread the new ideas that led to the Reformation. (1)
7. Deeply grateful to print, Luther said that printing was the ultimate and greatest gift of God. (1)

sst.text: Resource planning is called a complex process. Explain why. (3)
sst.answer:
Resource planning is complex because it has several stages that must all be done together:
(i) Resources have to be identified and listed across the regions of the country. This needs surveys, mapping, and measuring and estimating the resources both in quality and quantity. (1)
(ii) A planning structure has to be built, with the right technology, skills and institutions to carry out the resource plans. (1)
(iii) The plans for developing resources have to be matched with the overall national development plans. (1)
(iv) Planning is the accepted way to use resources wisely, so all these steps must be done with care. (1)
(Any three points, 1 mark each.)

sst.text:
Source subject: Joint Forest Management (JFM). In short: JFM has existed formally since 1988, when Odisha passed the first JFM resolution. Village institutions protect mostly degraded forest land managed by the forest department, and in return get non-timber forest produce and a share of the timber. The lesson is that local communities must be involved in managing natural resources.
(17.1) Why is it necessary to conserve forests? (1)
(17.2) What type of forests are protected under the Joint Forest Management programme? (1)
(17.3) Explain the role of local communities in conserving forests. (2)
sst.answer:
(17.1) Forests must be conserved to keep the ecological balance / to conserve wildlife. (Any one) (1)
(17.2) Degraded forests. (1)
(17.3) (i) In India, forests are home to some traditional communities, who protect them. (1)
(ii) People of five villages in the Alwar district of Rajasthan declared 1200 hectares of forest as the 'Bhairodev Dakav Sonchuri' and made their own rules for it. (1)
(iii) Local communities can work together with the government to conserve forests. (1)
(iv) Local communities can suggest methods of forest conservation. (1)
(v) They can organise movements such as the Chipko movement in the Himalayas, which resisted deforestation and promoted community afforestation, to make the public aware of the need to save forests. (1)
(Any two, 1 mark each.)

science.chapter: Ch 12 Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
science.text: What are magnetic field lines? Write two important properties of magnetic field lines. (2)
science.answer:
Magnetic field lines are the lines that represent the magnetic field around a magnet: they are the paths along which the north pole of a small compass needle would move, and the tangent at any point gives the direction of the magnetic field there (1).
Properties (any two) (½ + ½):
• No two field lines cross each other.
• Outside the magnet, field lines come out of the north pole and go into the south pole.
• Field lines are closed curves.
• Inside the magnet, the field lines go from its south pole to its north pole.

science.text: An object 5 cm tall is kept 30 cm from the optical centre of a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Using the lens formula, find the position and the size of the image. (3)
science.answer:
u = −30 cm, f = +20 cm, ho = 5 cm.
Position: lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (½)
1/v − 1/(−30) = 1/(+20) (½)
1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = (3 − 2)/60 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm (½).
The image is 60 cm from the lens, on the other side.
Size: m = hi/ho = v/u (½)
m = 60/(−30) = −2 (½)
hi = −2 × 5 cm = −10 cm. The image is 10 cm tall, inverted and enlarged (½).

science.text: The leaves of the sensitive plant move when they are touched. Explain this movement briefly. (2)
science.answer: When the plant is touched, its cells change shape by changing the amount of water in them. The cells swell or shrink, and this shows up as the movement of the leaves. (2)

sst.text: 'Recent evidence shows that overuse of groundwater is becoming a serious threat in many parts of the country.' Evaluate this statement in the context of sustainability of development. (5 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Sustainable development means economic development that does not damage the environment, and development today should not compromise the needs of future generations. (1)
2. Groundwater is a renewable resource; it is replenished by nature. (1)
3. Yet its overuse is becoming a serious threat in many parts of the country because of population growth and farming practices. (1)
4. Using too much groundwater for irrigation lowers the groundwater level. (1)
5. Without effective policies and regulation, groundwater is used in an unsustainable way. (1)
6. About 300 districts have reported a fall in the water level of more than 4 metres in the past 20 years. (1)
7. Nearly one-third of the country is overusing its groundwater reserves; in another 25 years, 60 per cent of the country would be doing the same if the present way of use continues. (1)
8. Overuse is found especially in agriculturally prosperous regions such as Punjab and Western Uttar Pradesh. (1)
9. Water must be used judiciously, and dumping of excess and toxic waste on land must be controlled so that groundwater is not polluted. (1)
(Write any five points.)

sst.text: 'In 1992 India took a major step towards decentralisation by bringing in local self-government through a Constitutional Amendment.' Support this statement with examples. (5)
sst.answer:
1. In 1992 the Constitution was amended to make the third tier of democracy more powerful and effective. (1)
2. It is now constitutionally compulsory to hold regular elections to local government bodies. (1)
3. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes in the elected bodies and among the executive heads of these institutions. (1)
4. At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women. (1)
5. An independent body, the State Election Commission, has been set up in each State to hold panchayat and municipal elections. (1)
6. State governments must share some powers and revenue with local government bodies; how much is shared varies from State to State. (1)
(Write any five.)

sst.text: Describe the distinctive role (functions) of political parties in a democracy. (5)
sst.answer:
1. Parties fill political offices and exercise political power. (1)
2. Parties contest elections. (1)
3. Parties put forward different policies and programmes, and the voters choose from them. (1)
4. Parties play a decisive role in making laws for the country. (1)
5. Parties form and run governments. (1)
6. Parties recruit leaders, train them and then make them ministers to run the government the way they want. (1)
7. Parties that lose elections play the role of opposition. (1)
8. Parties shape public opinion. (1)
9. Parties give people access to government machinery and to welfare schemes run by governments. (1)
(Write any five.)

sst.text: "The economic strength of a country is measured by the development of its manufacturing industries." Explain with examples. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) Manufacturing helps modernise agriculture, the backbone of our economy. (1)
(ii) It reduces people's heavy dependence on farm income by giving them jobs in the secondary and tertiary sectors. (1)
(iii) Industrial development is a precondition for removing unemployment and poverty; this was the main idea behind public sector industries and joint sector ventures in India. (1)
(iv) Setting up industries in tribal and backward areas was meant to reduce regional disparities. (1)
(v) Exports of manufactured goods expand trade and commerce and bring in foreign exchange. (1)
(vi) Countries that turn their raw materials into many finished goods of higher value are prosperous; India's prosperity lies in increasing and diversifying its manufacturing industries quickly. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)

sst.text: Explain, with examples, why using non-conventional sources of energy matters for the country. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) They are environment friendly. (1)
(ii) They are sustainable sources of energy. (1)
(iii) They are renewable. (1)
(iv) After the first cost, they become cheaper in the long run, since sunlight, wind and tides cost nothing, and they last long. (1)
(v) They are available in plenty. (1)
(vi) Examples: solar, wind and tidal energy. (1)
(vii) India depends heavily on coal, oil and gas; rising oil and gas prices and possible shortages threaten the security of our energy supply and the growth of the economy, so renewable sources reduce this dependence. (1)
(viii) Fossil fuels cause serious environmental problems; solar, wind, tidal, biomass and energy from waste reduce them. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)

science.text:
Give reasons: (3×1=3)
(i) In the extraction of metals, metal sulphides and carbonates should be changed into metal oxides.
(ii) Aluminium oxide is called an amphoteric oxide.
(iii) Metals like Na, K, Ca and Mg are never found free in nature.
science.answer:
(i) It is easier to get a metal from its oxide, because a metal oxide is easier to reduce to the metal. (1)
(ii) Aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and bases to give salt and water. (1)
(For example: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O and Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O)

science.text:
(a) Define one ampere.
(b) A wire of radius 0.01 cm has a resistance of 14 Ω. The resistivity of its material is 44 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. Find the length of the wire. (Take π = 22/7) (3)
science.answer:
(a) When 1 coulomb of charge flows through any cross-section of a conductor in 1 second, the current through it is 1 ampere; 1 A = 1 C / 1 s (1).
(b) r = 0.01 cm = 0.01 × 10⁻² m = 10⁻⁴ m; ρ = 44 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m; R = 14 Ω.
R = ρ l / A (½)
l = R × A / ρ = R × πr² / ρ (½)
l = 14 × (22/7) × (10⁻⁴)² / (44 × 10⁻⁸) = (44 × 10⁻⁸) / (44 × 10⁻⁸) = 1.0 m (1).

science.text: Explain the chlor-alkali process and write its chemical equation. Name the products formed at the anode and at the cathode. (3)
science.answer:
When electricity is passed through brine (aqueous sodium chloride), it breaks down to give sodium hydroxide (an alkali) and chlorine; so the process is called the chlor-alkali process. (1)
2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) →(electricity) 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) (1)
At the anode: chlorine gas, Cl₂ (½)
At the cathode: hydrogen gas, H₂; sodium hydroxide solution is formed near the cathode. (½)

sst.text: 'Sharing of power between the Union Government and the State Governments is basic to the structure of our Constitution.' Give arguments in support of this statement. (3)
sst.answer:
1. The Indian Constitution sets up different tiers of government: the Centre (Union) and the States. (1)
2. Each tier has its own jurisdiction, and this is specified in the Constitution. (1)
3. The Constitution has three lists (Union List, State List and Concurrent List) that give powers to each level. (1)
4. The fundamental provisions of the Constitution cannot be changed by one level of government on its own. (1)
5. Parliament cannot change this arrangement on its own: any change must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least a two-thirds majority and then ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the States. (1)
(Write any three.)

sst.text: Describe any three features of primitive subsistence farming. (3)
sst.answer:
(i) It is still practised in a few pockets of India. (1)
(ii) It is done on small patches of land. (1)
(iii) Primitive tools such as the hoe, dao and digging sticks are used. (1)
(iv) It depends on the monsoon. (1)
(v) It depends on the natural fertility of the soil and on other conditions being suitable for the crops grown. (1)
(vi) It uses family or community labour. (1)
(vii) It is 'slash and burn' agriculture: a patch of land is cleared and cropped; when its fertility falls, the farmers move to a new patch and leave the old one for nature to restore its fertility. (1)
(Any three, 1 mark each.)

sst.text: How did the movement to revive folklore help the growth of nationalist ideas in India? Explain with examples. (5)
sst.answer:
1. In late-nineteenth-century India, nationalists began recording folk tales sung by bards, and toured villages to gather folk songs and legends. (1)
2. They believed these tales gave a true picture of traditional culture, which had been corrupted and damaged by outside forces. (1)
3. Preserving this folk tradition was essential to discover one's national identity and restore a sense of pride in one's past. (1)
4. In Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore himself began collecting ballads, nursery rhymes and myths, and led the movement for folk revival. (1)
5. In Madras, Natesa Sastri published a massive four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales, The Folklore of Southern India; he believed folklore was national literature and the most trustworthy expression of people's real thoughts and character. (1)

sst.text: Describe the main characteristics of the cotton textile industry in India. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) In ancient India, cotton cloth was made by hand spinning and handloom weaving. (1)
(ii) Power looms came into use after the 18th century. (1)
(iii) In its early years the industry was concentrated in the cotton-growing areas. (1)
(iv) It is closely linked with agriculture and gives a living to farmers. (1)
(v) It gives jobs to cotton boll pluckers and to workers in ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing, designing, packaging, tailoring and sewing. (1)
(vi) By creating demand, it supports many other industries such as chemicals and dyes, packaging materials and engineering works. (1)
(vii) It adds to foreign trade and to the country's foreign exchange. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)

sst.text:
Source subject: the Sardar Sarovar Project. In short: the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada river in Gujarat is one of India's largest water projects, covering Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan. It will irrigate 18.45 lakh hectares covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat, 2,46,000 hectares in the desert districts of Barmer and Jalore (Rajasthan) and 37,500 hectares in the tribal hilly tract of Maharashtra; most of its command area is drought prone.
(18.1) Why is the Sardar Sarovar Project important for Gujarat? (1)
(18.2) Why has the project been designed to cover four states? (1)
(18.3) In what ways does this project promote sustainability? (2)
sst.answer:
(18.1) It gives irrigation to 18.45 lakh hectares of land, covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. (1)
(18.2) It is meant to meet the water needs of the drought-prone and desert areas (about 75% of its command area in Gujarat and all of it in Rajasthan are drought prone); it also gives irrigation to some areas of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra; the Narmada is an inter-state river, so the states share its water and the electricity it generates. (Any one) (1)
(18.3) (i) It provides drinking water to the drought-prone areas of these states. (1)
(ii) It irrigates large areas of farmland, giving food security to large populations. (1)
(iii) It generates hydroelectricity, a renewable and clean source of energy. (1)
(iv) It helps recharge groundwater, supporting sustainable water management. (1)
(Any two, 1 mark each.)

science.text: An object 5 cm tall is kept 30 cm from the optical centre of a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. Using the lens formula, find the position and the size of the image. (3)
science.answer:
u = −30 cm, f = +20 cm, ho = 5 cm.
Position: lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f (½)
1/v − 1/(−30) = 1/(+20) (½)
1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = (3 − 2)/60 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm (½).
The image is 60 cm from the lens, on the other side.
Size: m = hi/ho = v/u (½)
m = 60/(−30) = −2 (½)
hi = −2 × 5 cm = −10 cm. The image is 10 cm tall, inverted and enlarged (½).

science.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Metals can be refined by an electrochemical process: electrolysis is used to dissolve the metal and deposit it again selectively. Copper, zinc, tin, nickel, silver and gold are refined by this electrolytic method.
(a) What is anode mud? (1)
(b) In the electrolytic refining of copper, what are the anode and the cathode? (1)
(c) (i) Using chemical equations, show how copper is extracted from its ore Cu₂S. (2)
OR
(c) (ii) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the electrolytic refining of copper. (2)
science.answer:
(a) In electrolytic refining, the insoluble impurities that settle at the bottom below the anode are called anode mud. (1)
(b) Anode: a rod of impure copper (½); cathode: a strip of pure copper (½)
(c) (i) Cu₂S is heated in air: 2Cu₂S + 3O₂(g) →(heat) 2Cu₂O(s) + 2SO₂(g) (1)
The Cu₂O formed then reacts with more Cu₂S: 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S →(heat) 6Cu(s) + SO₂(g) (1)
OR
(c) (ii) Diagram (not drawn here): a tank of acidified copper sulphate solution; an impure copper anode and a pure copper cathode dipped in it and joined to a battery with a key; Cu²⁺ ions moving towards the cathode; impurities (anode mud) collected at the bottom below the anode. Labels: anode, cathode, acidified copper sulphate solution, tank, anode mud (impurities), key/battery. Diagram (1), labelling (1).

science.text:
(a) Why is it important that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix in birds and mammals? (1)
(b) Which animals can tolerate some mixing of the oxygenated and deoxygenated blood streams? What decides the body temperature of these animals? (1)
science.answer:
(a) Birds and mammals need a lot of energy to keep their body temperature constant. Keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate gives a highly efficient supply of oxygen to the body, which meets this need. (1)
(b) Amphibians / reptiles. (½) Their body temperature depends on the temperature of the environment. (½)

sst.chapter: E4 Globalisation and the Indian Economy
sst.text: 'Technology has stimulated the globalisation process.' Support this statement with examples. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor behind globalisation. (1)
2. Transport technology has made delivery of goods over long distances faster and cheaper. (1)
3. Containers have greatly reduced port handling costs. (1)
4. Air transport has become cheaper, so airlines carry much larger volumes of goods. (1)
5. Telecommunication, computers, the Internet, e-mail, voice-mail, fax and mobile phones are used to contact one another around the world. (1)
6. Information and communication technology lets us get information instantly and communicate even from remote areas. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.text: Why is the issue of sustainability important for development? Explain with examples. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Sustainability protects people against pollution and so keeps up their quality of life and health. (1)
2. Development needs the environment, so the environment must be conserved. (1)
3. Development can be kept going by using renewable resources such as groundwater, wind energy and solar energy. (1)
4. Even renewable resources can be overused. Groundwater is renewed by rain, but if we take out more than the rain puts back, we are overusing it. (1)
5. Non-renewable resources have a fixed stock on earth and get exhausted after years of use, so their overuse must be checked. (1)
6. New resources are discovered and add to the stock, but over time even these will be used up. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.text: Explain the measures that can be taken to reduce soil erosion. (2)
sst.answer:
(i) Contour ploughing: ploughing along the contour lines slows down the flow of water down the slopes. (1)
(ii) Terrace farming: steps (terraces) are cut on the slopes; terrace cultivation restricts erosion. (1)
(iii) Strip cropping: large fields are divided into strips and strips of grass are left to grow between the crops; this breaks the force of the wind. (1)
(iv) Shelter belts: rows of trees are planted to stop soil erosion. (1)
(Any two, 1 mark each.)

sst.text:
Source-based question titled 'An Experiment in Brazil'. In short, the source says: the city of Porto Alegre in Brazil set up a body alongside its municipal council in which its nearly 13 lakh people help make the city budget; each ward holds a meeting like a gram sabha that any resident can attend, and the proposals go to the municipality for a final decision.
(35.1) Explain what 'participatory democracy' means. (1)
(35.2) In the context of the division (sharing) of powers, this example describes which type of government? (1)

sst.answer:
(35.1) Participatory democracy means people take part in, or are directly involved in, the decision-making process. (1)
(35.2) Local self-government. (1)
(35.3) 1. Local self-government in India works through Panchayati Raj in villages, and Municipalities and Municipal Corporations in towns and cities. (1)
2. All bodies of local self-government are elected by the people. (1)
3. The gram sabha of the gram panchayat is a body where the people of the area take part directly. (1)
(Write any two for 35.3.)

sst.chapter: E4 Globalisation and the Indian Economy
sst.text: 'New technology has helped the world to become connected.' Justify this statement with suitable arguments. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Rapid improvement in technology has stimulated the globalisation process. (1)
2. Better transport technology has made delivery of goods over long distances much faster and cheaper. (1)
3. Developments in information and communication technology, especially telecommunications, computers and the Internet, let us get information instantly. (1)
4. These are used to contact one another around the world, to get information and to communicate from remote areas. (1)
5. Satellite communication devices have made global communication and sharing of information easier. (1)
6. Computers have entered almost every field, making information management and communication easier. (1)
7. The Internet lets us get and share information on almost anything and send instant e-mail and talk by voice-mail across the world at negligible cost. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.text: Why is sustainable development essential? Explain with examples. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Sustainable development is economic development that is friendly to the environment. (1)
2. Resources must be conserved for future generations. (1)
3. Resources should be used according to how much of them is available. (1)
4. Present needs must be met in a sustainable and judicious way. (1)
5. Scientists, economists, philosophers and other social scientists are working together for sustainable development. (1)
6. Example: groundwater is a renewable resource, renewed by nature like crops and plants, but it is being overused. (1)
7. Our future depends on essential resources, and these are being used up at a fast rate. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.text: Explain any three challenges faced by political parties in India. (3)
sst.answer:
1. Lack of internal democracy within parties: parties do not keep membership registers, hold organisational meetings or conduct internal elections regularly, so power gets concentrated in one or a few top leaders. (1)
2. Dynastic succession: top positions are held by members of one family, so ordinary workers rarely get a chance to rise to the top. (1)
3. Growing role of money and muscle power in parties, especially during elections: parties tend to nominate candidates who have or can raise a lot of money, and sometimes support criminals who can win elections. (1)
4. Lack of meaningful choice for the voters: the major parties do not differ much in their basic ideas and policies, so voters get little real choice. (1)
(Write any three, and explain each in a line.)

sst.text: Explain 'secularism' as laid down in the Indian Constitution. (2)
sst.answer:
1. There is no official religion for the Indian state. (1)
2. The Constitution gives all individuals and communities the freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion. (1)
3. The Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion. (1)
4. The Constitution allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities. (1)
(Write any two.)

sst.chapter: E2 Sectors of the Indian Economy
sst.text: Give any three suggestions to increase employment in rural areas and explain them. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Banks and cooperatives should give cheap and easy loans to farmers to buy inputs, so they can grow more and employ more people. (1)
2. Dams and canals should be built for irrigation, so that more land can be cultivated in more seasons. (1)
3. Transport and storage facilities should be improved; many people get work in transport and trade. (1)
4. Industries should be set up in semi-rural areas, for example dal mills and honey collection centres. (1)
5. Schools and health centres should be developed; they need teachers, doctors and other workers. (1)
6. Tourism and local crafts should be promoted. (1)
(Write any three points.)

science.text:
A ray of light goes from medium A into medium B. In the figure, the boundary between the two media is a horizontal line with a dashed normal drawn at the point where the ray meets it; medium A is below the boundary and medium B above. In medium A the ray travels at a large angle to the normal (almost along the surface); after crossing into medium B it travels much closer to the normal.
(a) Which of the two media is denser with respect to the other? Give a reason. (1)
(b) The speed of light is va in medium A and vb in medium B. What is the refractive index of medium B with respect to medium A? (1)
science.answer:
(a) Medium B is denser (½). In medium B the ray bends towards the normal, that is, the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence (∠r < ∠i) (½).
(b) Refractive index of B with respect to A: nBA = va / vb (1).

science.text:
(i) What is a homologous series? Which two of these organic compounds are in the same homologous series? C₂H₄, C₄H₁₀, C₃H₄, C₄H₈ (2)
(ii) Write the product(s) of these reactions: (2)
(I) CH₃–CH₂–OH + CH₃COOH →(acid)
(II) C₂H₅OH + O₂ →(burning)
(iii) Why do micelles form when soap is added to water? (1)
science.answer:
(i) A homologous series is a series of compounds in which the same functional group replaces hydrogen in a carbon chain; its members can be written with one general formula and successive members differ by a –CH₂ unit (14 u). (1)
C₂H₄ and C₄H₈ are in the same homologous series (both are alkenes). (1)
(ii) (I) CH₃CH₂OH + CH₃COOH →(acid) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (1)
(II) C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ →(burning) 2CO₂ + 3H₂O (1)
(iii) A soap molecule has an ionic end that dissolves in water and a long carbon chain (tail) that does not. In water the tails keep away from the water and come together inside a cluster, with the ionic ends on the outside facing the water; this cluster is a micelle. (With oil or dirt, the carbon chains hold the oil inside the micelle while the ionic ends stay in the water.) (1)

science.text: Give two main limitations of using electrical impulses as the way cells communicate in most multicellular animals. (2)
science.answer:
1. Electrical impulses reach only those cells that are connected by nervous tissue; not every cell of the body is connected to it. (1)
2. After a cell has generated and passed on an impulse, it needs some time to reset its mechanism before it can generate a new impulse. (1)

science.text: A circuit has a 2 V cell, a key K, and three resistors of 1 Ω, 2 Ω and 3 Ω, all joined one after another in series in a single loop. Using Ohm's law, find the potential difference across the 3 Ω resistor when the key is closed. (2)

"Every organism has two sets of all genes, one from each parent, so both parents contribute equally to the DNA of the offspring in sexual reproduction." If so, how does the DNA of the species stay stable (the same amount from generation to generation)? Discuss. (3)
science.answer:
• Each cell has two copies of each chromosome, one from the male parent and one from the female parent. (1)
• Each germ cell (gamete) takes only one chromosome from each pair (either the maternal or the paternal one). (1)
• When two germ cells fuse, the normal number of chromosomes is restored in the offspring, so the DNA of the species stays stable. (1)

sst.chapter: E4 Globalisation and the Indian Economy
sst.text: 'New technology has helped the world to become connected.' Justify this statement with suitable arguments. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Rapid improvement in technology has stimulated the globalisation process. (1)
2. Better transport technology has made delivery of goods over long distances much faster and cheaper. (1)
3. Developments in information and communication technology, especially telecommunications, computers and the Internet, let us get information instantly. (1)
4. These are used to contact one another around the world, to get information and to communicate from remote areas. (1)
5. Satellite communication devices have made global communication and sharing of information easier. (1)
6. Computers have entered almost every field, making information management and communication easier. (1)
7. The Internet lets us get and share information on almost anything and send instant e-mail and talk by voice-mail across the world at negligible cost. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.text: Why is the issue of sustainability important for development? Explain with examples. (3 marks)
sst.answer:
1. Sustainability protects people against pollution and so keeps up their quality of life and health. (1)
2. Development needs the environment, so the environment must be conserved. (1)
3. Development can be kept going by using renewable resources such as groundwater, wind energy and solar energy. (1)
4. Even renewable resources can be overused. Groundwater is renewed by rain, but if we take out more than the rain puts back, we are overusing it. (1)
5. Non-renewable resources have a fixed stock on earth and get exhausted after years of use, so their overuse must be checked. (1)
6. New resources are discovered and add to the stock, but over time even these will be used up. (1)
(Write any three points.)

sst.text: Describe the main characteristics of the cotton textile industry in India. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) In ancient India, cotton cloth was made by hand spinning and handloom weaving. (1)
(ii) Power looms came into use after the 18th century. (1)
(iii) In its early years the industry was concentrated in the cotton-growing areas. (1)
(iv) It is closely linked with agriculture and gives a living to farmers. (1)
(v) It gives jobs to cotton boll pluckers and to workers in ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing, designing, packaging, tailoring and sewing. (1)
(vi) By creating demand, it supports many other industries such as chemicals and dyes, packaging materials and engineering works. (1)
(vii) It adds to foreign trade and to the country's foreign exchange. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)

sst.text: Describe any three features of the Indian federal system. (3)
sst.answer:
1. There are two or more tiers (levels) of government; India has a government at the Centre (Union) and governments in the States. A third tier, local government (Panchayats and Municipalities), was added later. (1)
2. The different tiers govern the same citizens, but each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation and administration. (1)
3. The jurisdiction of each tier is specified in the Constitution. (1)
4. The fundamental provisions of the Constitution cannot be changed by one level of government alone. (1)
5. Courts have the power to interpret the Constitution, and the highest court acts as an umpire if there is a dispute between levels of government. (1)
6. The sources of revenue for each level of government are clearly specified. (1)
(Write any three.)

sst.text: Why is the per capita consumption of electricity taken as an index of development? Explain with examples. (5)
sst.answer:
(i) Electricity has such a wide range of uses in today's world that its per capita consumption is taken as an index of development. (1)
(ii) Electricity is needed in every sector of the economy. (1)
(iii) In agriculture, electric pumps lift water to irrigate fields, which raises output. (1)
(iv) The food processing industry needs electricity. (1)
(v) Cottage and small-scale industries cannot grow without electricity. (1)
(vi) Higher use of electricity in homes shows a higher standard of living. (1)
(vii) Development and the demand for electricity rise together. (1)
(Any five, 1 mark each.)
